Matt Pierce's January Newsletter Standing against paramilitary police in our neighborhoods, fighting for lower utility costs and more. Rep. Matt Pierce Jan 30, 2026 Share Welcome to my monthly newsletter, where I provide legislative updates as your state representative for House District 61. Please reach out to me at h61@iga.in.gov if you have any comments, questions, or concerns. I’m Strongly Opposed to Paramilitary Police in Our Communities House Bill 1343 is one of the most dangerous bills I’ve ever seen moving through the legislature. It’s playing with fire. It creates a national guard military police unit that the governor can deploy anywhere, whenever he thinks it’s necessary. The governor would be able to deploy a paramilitary force, without the full training required of civilian police, in our neighborhoods, the same way President Trump has deployed ICE units to Democrat-run cities. Local government officials would have no power to prevent this paramilitary force from invading their communities. I offered an amendment to HB 1343 that would have completely removed this provision from the bill, but my amendment was voted down by Republicans. What happens when you deploy a poorly trained paramilitary force in our communities? All you need to do is look at Minneapolis, Minnesota. You get a mother shot in the head after dropping her child off at school. You get a young ICU nurse shot in the back at point-blank range. You turn on the TV and see the videos, and you ask yourself, ‘How can this happen in our country?’ We see the tragedies that occur when one person has unchecked power. We are living in a time when the federal government is deploying paramilitary forces to communities it doesn’t like, and people are getting killed. Then, government officials lie to the American people about what happened. Why in God’s name would you give that kind of power to Indiana’s governor? The House should have rejected this dangerous bill. Unfortunately, the Republican supermajority passed the bill onto the Senate for further consideration. This is not who we are as Americans or Hoosiers. Watch my remarks about this bill on the House floor below: Fighting to Lower Your Utility Costs On Jan. 28, I voted for House Bill 1002 , a bill intended to make utility bills more affordable. I am pleased the House Republicans finally agreed to address this issue. Unfortunately, the bill is only a small step towards limiting increases in energy costs and expanding protections for utility customers. The bill at least does something, but more can be done. That’s why I offered two amendments to HB 1002. One amendment would have imposed a one-year moratorium on the 7% sales tax on utility bills with the expectation that it would be made permanent in the next budget. It also would have prevented the Indiana Economic Development Corporation (IEDC) from granting any further sales tax exemptions to data centers. House Republicans voted it down. Apparently, it’s fine for trillion-dollar corporations to pay no sales tax on energy use at their data centers. But not for Hoosier families to get the same tax break. My other amendment would have prohibited utility companies from making customers pay for their lobbying and political activities. House Republicans used a procedural move to avoid voting on the amendment. Republicans deemed the amendment unrelated to the contents of the bill, even though both concern how utility rates will be determined. They apparently want to continue making us pay for utility lobbying that works against our interests at the Statehouse rather than making their own shareholders pay for it. My fellow House Democrats also offered amendments to strengthen the bill. Each of the twelve amendments was voted down or tossed out by the majority party. Here are the proposed changes that were rejected: Amendment #4 : Allows Hoosiers to tap into low-cost energy through small-scale, community-based renewable energy projects. Amendment #5 : Protects medically vulnerable Hoosiers by prohibiting disconnections for individuals who have a certified medical condition that could result in severe illness or death in the event of a power outage. Amendment #6 : Requires utility companies to include certain information about payment assistance programs on the monthly bills of senior customers. Amendment #7 : Holds utilities accountable for reliable service by requiring they reimburse customers for any financial losses suffered as a result of an outage. Amendment #8 : Protects Hoosiers from private equity firms acquiring Indiana utility companies that lead to rate hikes. Amendment #10 : Creates a 1-year moratorium on the 7% sales tax on residential utility bills and prohibits IURC from issuing future tax breaks for data centers and quantum computing facilities. Amendment 11: Prohibits utilities from passing on the costs of lobbying and political activities to customers. This amendment was blocked on procedural grounds instead of being outright rejected. Amendment #13: Prohibits utility companies from raising utility rates more than 3% and requires utility companies to hold 3 public hearings in the affected utility service area before raising rates. Amendment #14 : Prohibits utility companies from disconnecting residential electric or natural gas service during the coldest time of year (beginning Dec. 1 and ending March 15). Amendment #15: Eliminates the 7% sales tax on residential utility bills. Amendment #16: Prohibits the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) from approving a rate increase above 3% of the average monthly bill. Amendment #19: Prohibits any increases in fixed rates and charges for utility bills for the next two years. (Effective June 30, 2026 to July 1, 2028). I appreciate that Republicans woke up this election year and discovered that people are struggling to pay their utility bills. Now, they’re doing at least a little something about it, but we could be doing much more to lessen the burden of skyrocketing utility bills. Here are the main provisions of HB 1002 as it passed the House: Performance-based Ratemaking Performance-based ratemaking ties rate and profit margin increases to the quality of service being provided, reliability, etc. However, the author of the bill stated that HB 1002 is not a full transition to basing our rates on performance. Multi-year Rate Plans: HB 1002 also refashions rate increases into three-year plans . Utility companies would implement a rate increase over three years instead of a single year. This prevents sharp increases and protects Hoosiers from being hit with repeated rate hikes. However, it doesn’t stop rate increases from happening. Block Service Shutoffs and Provide Additional Support for Vulnerable Hoosiers : In 2021, Indiana ranked third in the nation for utility disconnections. A provision in this bill prevents utility companies from shutting off electricity during extremely hot weather for customers who are eligible for and have applied for assistance under a heating assistance program. HB 1002 also requires utilities to offer some sort of low-income customer aid program but does not specify the form the program must take. These aid programs would be paid for with a portion of utility companies’ profits. Levelized Billing The legislation automatically enrolls all customers in levelized billing, which reduces fluctuations in monthly payments. Monthly charges are based on average usage, spreading the cost of utilities over many months so households pay a more consistent, predictable monthly bill. Levelized billing doesn’t reduce the cost of energy, but it helps families budget by spreading usage costs evenly. If you don’t want your bills levelized, you will be able to opt out. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) will need to ensure the process of periodically adjusting customers’ bills based on actual usage is fair. Working to Restore Faculty Governance and Alumni Elected Trustees On Jan. 29, I spoke in favor of an amendment offered by State Rep. Ed Delaney (D-Indianapolis) to House Bill 1408 that would have reversed the attacks on IU and higher education put in the 2025 budget bill at the last minute. It would have restored the three IU trustees elected by the alumni, restored faculty governance, and repealed the five-year productivity reviews of tenured faculty. I urged the House to pass the amendment, reminding them of how the provisions were placed in the budget bill at the last minute with no notice, no opportunity for public testimony, and no chance for legislators to offer amendments to the provisions. I also described my own experience as an IU faculty member and the many ways faculty were already reviewed before these laws were passed. I am disappointed the House Republicans rejected the amendment, but I will continue working to restore respect for IU faculty and the voice of alumni on the IU Board of Trustees. The Hoosiers Win, Google It The big news in January was the Indiana Hoosiers becoming the college football national champions. Coach Curt Cignetti, Fernando Mendoza, and the rest of the team all worked together to secure the win in Miami. They completed an undefeated 16-0 season, the first team to do so since the 1894 Yale Bulldogs. I’m proud to represent the district that is the home of the IU Bloomington campus and now the national champions. It was a fun storybook ride to the championship for all Hoosier fans. Congratulations to the Indiana Hoosiers, our 2025 College Football National Champions. Knowing Coach Cignetti, this won’t be the last time the title comes to IU. Matt Pierce's February Newsletter Fighting to unmask ICE, preserving local control over data centers and more. Rep. Matt Pierce Feb 28, 2026 Share Welcome to my monthly newsletter, where I provide legislative updates as your state representative for House District 61. Please reach out to me at h61@iga.in.gov if you have any comments, questions, or concerns. Republicans Rejected My Amendment to Unmask ICE On Feb. 16, I offered an amendment to Senate Bill 160. The amendment would have required the Law Enforcement Training Board to adopt a statewide policy prohibiting officers from wearing a mask during official duties, with exceptions for situations such as tactical operations and undercover work. It also would have made it a class A misdemeanor for a law enforcement officer to wear a mask with the intent to commit or conceal the commission of a criminal act. It would have applied to federal law enforcement agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). House Republicans voted down the amendment 33-59 . I asked Republicans what kind of country and state they want to live in today. Do we want to live in a nation or state where masked agents with no identification can stop and demand proof of citizenship, and then arrest and send us off to a distant detention center? I don’t want to live in that kind of state or country. I don’t want to live in a place where masked agents demand to see your papers on the street. That is a big step towards authoritarian government. Republicans love to talk about the dangers of big government. We hear complaints about interference with property rights or too much regulation of businesses. Yet masked agents on the streets of America violating the constitutional rights of its residents, including unjustifiable killings, are met with deafening silence. This amendment was a chance for the General Assembly to stand up and demand that the federal government respect our freedoms and liberties. Instead, Republicans said ‘no’ to preserving what so many of us took for granted. Rep. Pierce presenting his amendment on the House floor. SUCCESS: Language Supporting Data Centers Removed From Bill Earlier this month, House Republicans passed House Bill 1333 . They voted to open up certain portions of Indiana’s farmland to large projects that could include data centers, oil refineries or smelting plants. In HB 1333, if the soil quality is poor, these projects can move forward automatically, without public hearings or community input. This vote further weakens local control and shuts Hoosiers out of decisions that affect their own communities. Supporters of the bill admitted it was too broad, but they hoped the Senate would fix it. Thankfully, Hoosiers spoke up, resulting in the bill not moving forward in the Senate. Thousands of people called, emailed and posted about the bill on social media. Your voice changed the outcome of this legislation. This is proof that our collective power can make a big difference in issues big and small. I hope you continue to stay engaged and stay vocal as we fight for an Indiana that puts people above the needs of corporations. The IURC is Investigating High Utility Bills: They Should Study Republican’s Legislation On Feb. 25, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) announced an “Investigative Inquiry on Energy Affordability” on March 24, calling in the five largest investor-owned utilities in the state to present on various topics related to energy affordability. The five utilities presenting include AES Indiana, CenterPoint Energy Indiana, Duke Energy Indiana, LLC, Indiana Michigan Power Company, and Northern Indiana Public Service Company, LLC. I’m calling on the IURC to expand the scope of its investigation to include the impact on rates of legislation passed by the Indiana General Assembly. I am pleased the IURC is responding to Hoosiers’ concerns about skyrocketing utility bills, but this investigation will be incomplete if it doesn’t include an honest assessment of how policies adopted by the Indiana House and Senate have contributed to unaffordable bills. They should look at the following legislation from Indiana Republicans : Senate Enrolled Act 560 (2013) created the Transmission, Distribution, and Storage Improvement Charge (TDSIC), which allows utilities to immediately charge consumers for 80% of the cost of system improvements without going through a rate case. House Enrolled Act 1470 (2019) reversed a court ruling that the IURC had been too generous in approving TDSIC requests by the utilities, including approving items that did not benefit consumers. The legislature quickly rewrote the TDSIC laws to ensure the utilities received what they requested. HEA 1417 (2023) overturned a Supreme Court decision that ruled the IURC had improperly allowed customers to be charged for $212 million in coal-ash cleanup. SEA 340 (2014) and SEA 412 (2015) killed Indiana’s energy efficiency program, Energizing Indiana, that benefited consumers by reducing consumption by 399,432 megawatt hours of electricity (enough to power 37,886 homes for a year), and offered assistance with weatherizing homes and purchasing energy-efficient appliances. SEA 309 (2017) ended net metering in Indiana, making it more difficult for Hoosiers to produce their own energy through rooftop solar. HEA 1420 (2023) gave monopoly utilities a right of first refusal to control the construction of expensive transmission lines rather than allowing outside companies to competitively bid on these projects, ultimately paid for by utility customers. HEA 1421 (2023) and SEA 271 (2022) allow construction work in progress (CWIP) for natural gas and small modular reactors. This forces customers to pay for generation plants before they provide any power and shifts the risk of cost overruns onto the backs of utility customers. Decades of Republican-controlled utility policy have led us to where we are today. At every turn, the Statehouse Republican supermajority chose the profit margins of investor-owned utility companies over everyday Hoosiers. The IURC should not ignore the actions of the General Assembly that have opened the door to higher utility rates.
